title: Engage participants digitally
overview:
If club members cannot access their regular facilities, they are likely to feel disconnected from one another and have limited access to training equipment. In these situations, sports clubs can use digital alternatives to stay connected, active, and supportive by providing adapted forms of training online.

Live-streamed or recorded training sessions are a good alternative to keep members motivated and connected to the club and one another. In addition, coaches can create simple fitness challenges or skill drills, which members can participate in by digitally sharing or documenting their efforts (e.g. sharing photos or results or GPS tracking). This can help provide motivation and routine across the group.

In addition, the use of messaging platforms, social media and/or club apps help maintain regular communication with all members and provide a sense of belonging to the club and its values.

During times of crisis, when normal participation in sport is not possible, digital tools allow clubs to keep promoting physical activity, well-being and community in flexible and inclusive ways.

guidelines.heading: Ensure accessibility and familiarity of digital tools
items: Start using digital communication tools in normal times so that staff and participants are already familiar with the tool when a crisis occurs.
Use existing digital tools that are intuitive and/or that people are already familiar with.
Make sure the tools you use are mobile-friendly and free for participants to use.

guidelines.heading: Create clear communication spaces
items: Create one or multiple digital communication spaces for everyday informal communication, where participants can easily share thoughts, updates, photos, and messages to motivate and build community.
Live meetings or training sessions can be used to create moments together and give structure, e.g. video conferencing.

guidelines.heading: Set relevant rules and structure
items: Set expectations for how participants could engage through digital communication tools, for example by providing a short online guide and a code of conduct.
Propose fixed days or times for activity to help create structure during periods of uncertainty.

guidelines.heading: Encourage participation
items: Set fun challenges, with focus on effort and participation over performance.

guidelines.heading: Provide support and follow-up
items: Designate someone in your team to provide technical support to staff and participants to avoid frustration, exclusion or disengagement.
Check in on participants individually who are not engaging.

guidelines.heading: Ensure safety
items: Take steps to ensure the safety and privacy of individuals and their data. For example use a tool that does not show participants each other’s phone numbers if necessary. Make sure video links are not publicly accessible.

cooperation_guidance: Speak to other sport clubs and organisations to find out which digital tools they recommend.
Many digital tools are free, or provide discounts for charities and clubs, it may be beneficial to make contact with the provider(s) of the digital tool to find out what your options are.

Screenshot of a group chat where people are sharing photos or messages of their training

case_example.context: Minor Ndako Sport is a sports club in Brussels, Belgium that used digital engagement to keep their running group going during the COVID-19 pandemic.
key_approaches: We used a private Strava club to help young refugees in Brussels see each other’s runs, give kudos, and feel connected during the COVID-19 pandemic.
We set simple challenges to encourage regular participation and routine when group training was not possible.
We celebrated effort, consistency, and personal milestones to keep motivation high during periods of restriction and isolation.
We shared routes, ideas, and suggested sessions around Brussels to inspire each other when running alone.
We used agreed virtual run days so participants feel they are running together, even when apart.
case_example.quote: [During the pandemic], since we weren’t allowed to run in group anymore, we created a 50 km challenge: everyone ran individually and tried to complete 50 km during December 2020. Every time you went for a run, you either sent a photo in WhatsApp or posted it on Strava.
case_example.outcome: This approach helped us stay motivated, engaged, and connected despite lockdowns and the lack of in-person activity.

title: Upskill coaches on mental wellbeing
overview:
External crises can significantly affect the mental health of sport participants. They may face disrupted routines, isolation, physical danger, financial stress, loss of stability, or trauma. As a result, some may stop participating in sport.

To prevent this and keep sport a positive space for mental wellbeing, coaches need ongoing training to respond to evolving mental health challenges. Through their attitudes and training methods, they play a key role in helping participants benefit from sport in a supportive environment.

guidelines.heading: Embrace supportive coaching practices
items: Promote a healthy approach to sport, focusing on enjoyment, wellbeing, and abilities rather than performance pressure or body appearance as only and primary drivers.
Build trust with sport participants and create a safe team environment where participants feel supported, including through peer support.

guidelines.heading: Provide a positive working environment for coaches, including support, learning opportunities and a healthy work-life balance
items: Provide regular training to help coaches respond to changing challenges.
Make sure coaches can have mental health support, within the organisation or with external support contacts.

guidelines.heading: Involve external support contacts when necessary for professional help
items: Give resources and structure for coaches to remain in their responsibilities scope and seek external help for sport participants when needed.

cooperation_guidance: Partner with providers of mental health awareness training or mental health first aid training for coaches and staff and see what training they recommend and can offer.
Identify and contact local mental health services or associations who can advise or take over the support of an individual when needed.
Work with other clubs in your area to share coach training to reduce costs and allow more sessions.

title: Invest in volunteer capacity
overview:
External crises can cause volunteers to leave because of changing priorities, stress, lack of resources, uncertainty or health and safety concerns. This disrupts operations and erodes critical skills and community connections, undermining an organisation’s ability to function effectively.

Investing in volunteers’ capacity, through training, recognition and support, fosters engagement and a sense of belonging. This helps clubs retain and attract volunteers, ensuring stability and resilience to navigate crises and achieve long-term growth.

guidelines.heading: Volunteer engagement — develop competences
items: Support volunteers in developing skills that are useful both within and outside the club.
Assess volunteers’ skills regularly to identify knowledge or skills gaps.
Provide accessible training opportunities such as workshops, webinars, online materials, and practical sessions.
Facilitate access to formal certifications such as coaching or refereeing certifications.
Encourage peer learning by creating moments where volunteers share their knowledge and experience.

guidelines.heading: Volunteer engagement — show appreciation
items: Regularly thank volunteers for their time and contribution.
Publicly recognise volunteers through events, social media or small awards.
Formalise the roles with role titles and role descriptions.

guidelines.heading: Volunteer engagement — support involvement
items: Offer flexible volunteering options, including short-term, long-term and remote roles.
Adapt tasks to match volunteers’ availability and capacity.
Support volunteers’ wellbeing by being attentive to stress, time constraints and crisis situations.
Involve volunteers in decision-making processes related to club activities.

guidelines.heading: Role management — structure responsibilities
items: Define clear and simple role descriptions so each volunteer understands their tasks and responsibilities.
Set up a structured onboarding process that includes welcoming new volunteers, providing simple guides or checklists, and assigning a mentor or buddy.

guidelines.heading: Role management — ensure stability
items: Identify and prepare replacements for key roles in advance.
Organise shadowing opportunities so new volunteers can learn from experienced members.
Ensure proper handover of tasks and responsibilities when volunteers leave their role.

guidelines.heading: Role management — manage information
items: Centralise all key information using shared digital tools.
For example, store essential documents including guides, meeting notes, decisions, contact lists and calendars.
Document important processes so that tasks can be easily continued by others.
Use simple and clear formats to ensure all information is easy to understand and use.

guidelines.heading: Communication and club culture — share information clearly
items: Clearly communicate the organisation’s mission, values, and priorities through simple documents and regular updates.
Maintain regular communication through short meetings, emails, newsletters, or social media.

guidelines.heading: Communication and club culture — build a positive environment
items: Create opportunities for open discussion and actively collect feedback from volunteers.
Use feedback to improve club practices and decision-making.
Organise social and informal activities to strengthen relationships between members and volunteers.
Promote a welcoming and inclusive environment for all participants.

cooperation_guidance: Build connection with relevant local training course providers who could support the skill development of your staff and volunteers.
Find out about local networks and platforms for recruiting new volunteers (e.g. universities network, municipalities network).
Work with other clubs in your area to share trainings to reduce costs and allow more sessions.
Build partnerships with schools, municipalities or local organisations to support recruitment and engagement of volunteers.

title: Diversify funding
overview:
External crises disrupt sports club funding streams by reducing revenue (e.g. cancelled events, lower membership fees) and cutting financial support (e.g. withdrawn sponsorships, reallocated public funds), while also increasing costs (e.g. repairs, safety measures). This creates a double pressure of less income and higher expenses.

Diversifying funding sources can guarantee more financial stability during uncertain times for the organisation. Grants, partnerships or community initiatives allow the club to rely on different incomes, should one source of money disappear.

guidelines.heading: Assess your financial situation and define your needs
items: Conduct a financial assessment (internally or with an external expert) to review revenue streams, cost structures and financial risks.
Define financial needs and goals with the minimum income required for operations and future spending to set fundraising goals.
Assess the legal structure of your organisation to identify revenue options available in your region, country or at national and European level.

guidelines.heading: Use tools to organise and optimise your financial strategy
items: Use existing business models to map current and potential revenue streams.
Establish clear policies for spending limits, approval processes and accountability mechanisms.

guidelines.heading: Get ready with a contingency fund
items: Build and maintain a reserve fund to prepare for unexpected financial shortfalls.

guidelines.heading: Diversify your revenue streams
items: Prioritise diversified income sources beyond membership fees such as events, sponsorships, grants and facility rentals.
Expand partnerships outside your regular network such as local businesses for sponsorships and advertising (e.g. website, event programmes, facilities).
Use all your assets at their fullest, such as renting out spaces during your activities or offering services to external users during events or specific activities.

guidelines.heading: Strengthen your team’s financial expertise
items: Train or recruit volunteers/staff with financial expertise to strengthen oversight and decision-making.

cooperation_guidance: Work in partnership with financial or business development experts to do the financial assessment and to develop alternative income generation.

Attract new partners and build trust with members, sponsors, and stakeholders through transparency and accountability and through external communication, such as public campaigns or a yearly report of activities.
Collaborate with other sectors beyond sport.

title: Use Digital Communication Tools
overview:
External crisis can disrupt in-person activity, and thereby day-to-day communication within the club. Developing resilient communication practices is essential for sport clubs to navigate crises effectively, even when activity is on hold. Using digital communication channels allows you to retain membership and community. This way, when the situation allows, regular activity can return as quickly as possible, without the loss of staff, volunteers, or members along the way.

Many clubs already rely on digital tools for everyday coordination among staff, volunteers, and members, and these same tools can become indispensable during times of disruption.

To strengthen internal communication, clubs should establish simple, consistent channels for sharing information, reassure your community and hear from members.

guidelines.heading: Choose the right tools — before a crisis hits
items: Match the tool to the purpose: informal updates (WhatsApp, Messenger, Slack, Teams), formal communication (email, newsletters, community posts), and shared planning (Notion, Asana, Obsidian, intranet).
Build in two-way channels — polls, feedback forms, open discussion spaces — so members and volunteers can raise concerns and feel ownership.
Prioritise accessibility: mobile-friendly, free, available in the local language, and safe with participants’ data.
Introduce these tools in normal times, using platforms people already know, so everyone is comfortable with them well before a crisis occurs.

guidelines.heading: Assign clear roles
items: Designate one person or team responsible for official communication, and clarify who manages which channel to avoid confusion.
Set up smaller informal groups (volunteers, coaches, parents, specific teams) for targeted updates.

guidelines.heading: Build the skills to use them well
items: Offer short, practical training on messaging, shared drives, and scheduling tools — peer-led demos tied to everyday tasks work best.
Help staff write clear, audience-appropriate updates, using simple templates to keep a consistent tone.
Keep building capacity over time: peer support, refresher sessions, and reusable “how-to” guides embed these skills so communication holds up under pressure.

cooperation_guidance: Speak to other sport clubs and organisations to find out which digital tools they recommend.
Many digital tools are free, or provide discounts for charities and clubs, it may be beneficial to make contact with the provider(s) of the digital tool to find out what your options are.

title: Build a strategy
overview:
External crises can disrupt operations, strain resources and create uncertainty, creating challenges for sports organisations to adapt, innovate and retain staff and volunteers.

Strategic planning provides solid foundations to navigate these challenges by fostering a sense of belonging and aligning day-to-day operations with long-term goals and organisational values, while empowering teams when facing limited human, financial or physical capacities. Embedding resilience into the strategy allows organisations to not only endure uncertain times but also thrive.

guidelines.heading: Define a clear strategic direction, informed by analysis and regularly reviewed
items: Articulate a clear vision, mission, and long-term objectives to guide the club’s direction.
Co-define specific objectives with staff and volunteers, and review them periodically.
Conduct an analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT analysis), covering internal and external factors, to inform decisions.
In a crisis, work with the team to re-articulate the core purpose and set a strategy for continuing to deliver on the organisation’s objectives.

guidelines.heading: Embed inclusive, structured strategic planning into organisational processes
items: Assign dedicated time and responsibility for strategic planning, separate from daily operations.
Integrate strategic planning into existing structures — staff meetings, events, stakeholder consultations.
Engage key stakeholders (staff, volunteers, coaches, members, parents, community partners) throughout the process.
Set engagement goals that build ownership, alignment, and shared commitment.

guidelines.heading: Translate innovative planning into actionable plans
items: Encourage creative, flexible thinking during planning.
Use non-formal methods — simulations, brainstorming, team-building — to support this.
Explore new programmes, partnerships, and delivery models.
Turn strategic objectives into SMART action plans, i.e. Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound actions.

guidelines.heading: Ensure effective implementation and adaptation through capacity-building, monitoring, and communication
items: Strengthen leadership and management skills through training and peer learning with other organisations.
Embed monitoring and evaluation — KPIs, regular reviews — into governance processes.
Communicate the strategic plan clearly and consistently to all stakeholders.
Reflect the organisation’s values and objectives in external communication, for example, demonstrating the inclusion of vulnerable groups.

cooperation_guidance: External facilitators can be an asset to help give fairness and weight to all voices and ideas. Consider using this as an opportunity to invite a local organisation, business or consultant who can help support the process of developing a strategy, but also hold the organisation accountable to implementing the plans.
You may find that there are official business or sport management advisory organisations who offer this sort of support for free.
Once the mission and objectives of the organisation are clear, think carefully about who can help the organisation in achieving these objectives.

title: Build relationships in the community
overview:
The community network becomes a critical source of support when crisis strikes, so it is recommended that grassroots sport clubs build and maintain a mix of formal and informal external relationships. Strong ties, cultivated well before disruption hits, give clubs somewhere to turn for emergency support, faster information-sharing, and continuity when routine channels break down.

Personal connections within the community are key to establishing partnerships with sponsors, facility providers, and other local stakeholders — relationships should be active, mutually beneficial, and reliable to ensure long-term collaboration.

Clubs also need to navigate more bureaucratic partners, such as local government, media, or regional sport organisations. Understanding and responding to their requirements is critical for sustaining support and accessing resources.

guidelines.heading: Identify, analyse and diversify partnerships
items: Map potential external partners (sponsors, facility providers, local government, media, local sport organisations, funding bodies).
Analyse the benefits, common goal, and what your club can offer in return.
Allow for diverse partnerships, i.e. include both informal community contacts and formal organisational relationships.
Ensure relationships are well balanced, i.e. avoid overreliance on a single partner, and ensure both parties are benefitting from the relationship.

guidelines.heading: Build trust
items: Leverage personal connections to initiate partnerships and build trust.
Develop long-lasting partnerships by identifying shared values and strategic objectives.
Invite partners to visit, watch or experience the work you do.

guidelines.heading: Document, engage and evaluate
items: Create documentation on key contacts, agreements and processes to maintain institutional knowledge in case of staff changes.
Maintain engagement through regular communication, updates and joint activities.
Monitor and evaluate partnerships regularly (e.g. yearly reports or meetings) and adjust strategies to maximise the relationships.

guidelines.heading: Strengthen skills and apply strategies
items: Train club leadership and/or volunteers in management of partnership and negotiation skills.
Plan how bureaucratic partnerships will be managed to access funding and resources effectively.
Use practical strategies, such as asking for small favours to build goodwill, while avoiding direct financial requests.

cooperation_guidance: Identify networks and events where you can raise awareness about your organisation, meet other organisational leaders, but also communicate your current needs in a partnership.
Invite your club members to use their network and personal connections to support you.

title: Target parents to reach socio-economically vulnerable children
overview:
Engaging parents in sport accessibility efforts is critical, as economic challenges during crises lead to reduced spending on children’s activities, which disproportionately affects lower-income families and worsens health inequalities. Clubs must be proactive as not all parents will feel that they can ask for support. Appointing a dedicated intermediary at a local sport club can help parents navigate funding options, monitor progress, and reduce dropout during referral processes.

Clubs should actively collaborate with organisations that provide financial aid to streamline referrals and make support to families more efficient and user-friendly.

guidelines.heading: Reduce barriers to entry
items: Build financial support into planning, such as lower membership fees for low-income families.
Focus support on arranging sports participation for children, not on other challenges parents or families may be facing — gathering broader information can cause distrust of institutions.
Address hidden costs like transport and kit through solutions like car-sharing, public transport options, or free/second-hand/rental equipment.

guidelines.heading: Make support easy to find and access
items: Share accessible materials (flyers, online resources) in places parents regularly visit — schools, community centres, healthcare facilities.
Create simple referral pathways between clubs and external support organisations to minimise delays, bureaucracy, or confusion.
Appoint a dedicated liaison to guide parents through financial support processes.

guidelines.heading: Build trust and reduce stigma
items: Train staff and volunteers to offer supportive, non-judgmental guidance that reduces the risk of shame or distrust among parents.
Launch communication campaigns that normalise financial barriers and reinforce that seeking support is common and acceptable.

guidelines.heading: Monitor outcomes
items: Track participation outcomes (e.g. comparing initial requests from families to actual participation) to ensure interventions are reducing dropout and increasing engagement among vulnerable groups.

cooperation_guidance: Establish formal partnerships or collaborations with organisations providing financial aid to ensure easier access to funds for your members. Such collaboration might include awareness raising events and info days or creating materials on existing support programmes.
Work closely with schools for arranging referrals of children or families that might face access issues.

title: Organise informed activities for refugees
overview:
When a crisis forces people to leave their homes and their country, welcoming sport clubs can offer people a way to heal. Grassroots sport organisations should provide free, culturally responsive, and trauma-informed services to remove financial and social barriers for disadvantaged and displaced communities.

Programmes should be designed through experience-based co-design with target participants, ensuring attention to cultural safety, emotional safety, community connection, accessibility, physical activity literacy, and support for basic needs.

Creating physical spaces that foster cultural and emotional safety — including interpreters, privacy options and services covering basic needs — can enhance participation.

guidelines.heading: Deliver culturally responsive, trauma-informed care
items: Understand the culture, needs, fears and experiences of the community or communities you are looking to engage.
Adapt current activities to be safe for people with experiences of trauma.
Train staff and volunteers on intercultural competencies to understand the target group’s culture, including gender provisions.
Maintain physical spaces that promote cultural and emotional safety, including interpreter services and optional privacy elements (e.g. window blinds, prayer rooms).

guidelines.heading: Ensure accessibility
items: Consider geographic proximity and accessibility of facilities. For example, deliver activity where the participants live or organise transportation.
Train and support coaches to adapt sessions and communication in response to language barriers. Translate key documents or communication.

cooperation_guidance: Involve the community in design. Co-create programming with the target group and engage families and community leaders where possible.

Relationships with community organisations, health services and refugee organisations are important for improving referral pathways, providing specialised training, and offering additional resources such as clothing, transport, translation or childcare support.
Consider partnering with other non-profit or humanitarian organisations for joint programming that balances physical activity with broader support needs.

title: Create networks for advocacy
overview:
Sport organisations should leverage political capital to enhance resilience during crises by actively engaging with and influencing political decision-makers. This is especially important because many clubs rely on government agencies for funding and support, yet often face power imbalances in negotiations.

Coordinated actions, such as joint representations with other sport organisations, are more effective than pursuing individual interests. By collaborating collectively, organisations can strengthen their voice, increase access to resources, and improve outcomes during times of crisis.

guidelines.heading: Make a strong case
items: Develop clear, evidence-based arguments focused on community impact and social value. Sport’s impact is transversal — it contributes to economy, education, health, and other sectors — so use this to connect with stakeholders across those areas.
Gather views and ideas from your members to give voice to them, to ensure your proposals are relevant and to strengthen your case.
Ensure your proposals and advocacy efforts are in line with your strategic purpose and values. This advocacy work should complement and support your goals.

guidelines.heading: Understand the political landscape
items: Identify key political stakeholders — local, regional, and national government agencies that influence funding, regulations, and support for your sport.
Monitor policy developments, government priorities, and funding opportunities relevant to your field, so advocacy efforts align with current political agendas.

guidelines.heading: Build and sustain relationships
items: Build and maintain relationships with decision-makers through regular communication, meetings, and participation in relevant committees or forums.
Document interactions, agreements, and commitments with political stakeholders to preserve institutional memory despite personnel changes.

guidelines.heading: Build organisational capacity for advocacy
items: Integrate political engagement and advocacy into your broader communication strategy, crisis management, and strategic planning processes.
Train staff or volunteers in advocacy, negotiation, and stakeholder engagement.
Establish formal mechanisms for ongoing political engagement, such as advisory boards, working groups, or liaison roles. Evaluate the effectiveness of these strategies regularly.

cooperation_guidance: Collaborate with other sport organisations to make joint representations or collective proposals to increase and influence credibility during negotiations and for joining advocacy campaigns.

Building strong relationships with public and government bodies during normal times means that these agencies will already know the value your club offers, and you will be better placed to ask for help or support during times of crisis to continue serving your community.

title: Adapt outdoor activities to changing climate
overview:
Global warming and associated natural disasters can disrupt sport activity or introduce risks to participants’ health and safety. Consider your preparation and response to temperature changes, weather events as well as reduced air quality.

“Europe has the highest excess death rates per 100,000 due to heat exposure.” — Monash University, 2021

There are various approaches to adapt your activities in case of a natural disaster or extreme weather events. Sport organisations can enhance safety and comfort through structural modifications such as shaded areas, water features, and climate-resilient infrastructure in sports facilities.

Sports organisations could prioritise flexible scheduling of outdoor activities and encourage healthy habits, including proper hydration and UV protection.

guidelines.heading: Safe guidelines and scheduling
items: Create internal guidelines for when it’s safe to practice, with reasonable adjustments to keep sport possible in new conditions (e.g. training in the rain, moving indoors, shorter and more frequent sessions in heat).
Adjust outdoor training and competition to cooler times of day, avoiding peak heat or poor air quality.
Build flexible programming that allows last-minute changes or cancellations based on weather and environmental alerts.
Implement air quality monitoring for outdoor activities and communicate risks clearly to staff, athletes, and participants.

guidelines.heading: Adapt facilities and infrastructure
items: Install or increase shaded areas, cooling zones, and access to water (fountains, misting systems) in sports and play spaces; promote hydration and UV-protective clothing and equipment.

Where possible, incorporate or advocate for heat-resilient, climate-proof infrastructure — e.g. permeable surfaces to reduce flooding, materials that minimise heat retention, and green solutions like tree planting and natural shade in facility planning.

guidelines.heading: Build awareness and community resilience
items: Educate coaches, staff, athletes, and families on climate risks and adaptive behaviours through training and awareness programmes.

cooperation_guidance: Reach out to environmental organisations to collaborate on initiatives and events to raise awareness on the effects of climate change.

Collaborate with local authorities, partners and the community to advocate for policies and urban design approaches that support heat-safe spaces, improved air quality monitoring, and accessible cooling stations.

Involve members, volunteers, and local residents in the community to shape and implement climate resilience — for example, gathering input on where shade or water points are most needed, or having them volunteer in local tree-planting.
image_ideas: Picture of athletes continuing practice in heavy rain

case_example.context: World Athletics uses city marathons as a platform to measure and raise awareness of urban air pollution. With more than a million marathon participants globally each year, the project leverages existing running communities to spark positive transformations within cities and increase awareness of air quality issues. Frequent runners are disproportionately exposed to air pollution — they spend more time outdoors, breathe more air, and tend to mouth-breathe during exertion, bypassing the nose’s natural filtration, so more pollutants reach the lungs, heart, and brain.
key_approaches: World Athletics installs air quality monitoring devices in selected cities for six months, gathering hyperlocal data specifically reflecting the air exercising individuals are exposed to — measured at around 2 metres in height, unlike most existing sensors which focus on traffic monitoring or regulatory compliance.

For six months before the marathon, a fixed device records background pollution trends at a location chosen with local stakeholders and informed by running-app data, targeting existing outdoor exercise hotspots like parks, riversides, or promenades.
During the marathon itself, a device attached to a bicycle follows the route in real time to capture fluctuations along the course and at the finish line.

Pollutant gases and particulates, alongside climate data (temperature, humidity, dew point, wind direction, wet bulb globe temperature), are translated into an Air Quality Index and Heat Stress Index that are reported live online for local stakeholders.
case_example.outcome: Key cooperations: Clean Air Fund (funding), Kunak Technologies (air monitoring equipment) and Strava Metro (monitoring data).

title: Prepare for disaster recovery
overview:
Sport organisations should strengthen organisational resilience by preparing for disaster recovery. Ensuring that the organisation can mobilise members and volunteers may be central to recovery efforts. Research on disaster recovery in grassroots sport shows that organisations facing crisis should proactively pursue government grants and subsidies, as well as ensure timely access to financial support, which has a significant positive effect on recovery outcomes. Clubs are encouraged to secure appropriate insurance coverage, particularly for high-risk assets like outdoor facilities, since this resource is often underutilised. Organisations should also consider the implications of facility ownership versus rental, as clubs responsible for their own facilities may face greater reconstruction challenges. Improving the substitutability of resources through role documentation, diversified income sources, and access to alternative facilities can reduce dependency on single points of failure and support more effective recovery.

Clubs should also continue communicating and engaging with their members and local community, even when activity is not possible, to minimise drop-out rates and so that recovery is quick and smooth once activity may resume.

items: Human resources are the most used resource in recovery, and capacity to mobilise members and volunteers is critical to club functioning, especially after disasters. Establish communication channels to inform and engage your volunteers and members in recovery efforts.
Proactively pursue government grants and subsidies in case of a natural disaster and ensure suitable insurance coverage, particularly for likely impacted areas (e.g. outdoor facilities).

In order to prepare for potential crises, consider that facility ownership significantly affects recovery: clubs responsible for their own facilities may face greater recovery challenges since they must manage reconstruction, while facilities owned by governments or private entities may be repaired by those entities.

Recognise differences in recovery across sport types. Research shows that some sports may face greater barriers to recovery from a natural disaster — examples might include motor sports, equestrian, and golf clubs that are prone to a slower recovery.

Dependence on single resources (people, funding, facilities) may weaken recovery capacity. Improve substitutability of resources to reduce dependence on specific individuals or resources: use written job descriptions and manuals for human resources, diversify income (e.g. donations, sponsorship) for financial resources, and build relationships with partners for access to alternative facilities.

cooperation_guidance: Connect with national/state sport organisations to inquire about available support in case of a natural disaster.
Build relationships with other sport organisations and community spaces for access to alternative facilities.

case_example.organization: Glenmore Lodge — Scotland’s National Outdoor Training Centre
case_example.context: In July 2026, a major wildfire broke out in the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland, putting Glenmore Lodge — the national outdoor training centre — inside the evacuation zone for several weeks. The multi-agency response successfully protected the lodge itself, and the facility officially reopened despite the loss of ancient woodland and landscapes.
key_approaches: The sport centre referred to emergency services rather than making independent safety calls. They told clients not to travel to the area and to follow official fire service advice.
Staff from Glenmore Lodge stayed on-site during the closure to assist emergency crews and coordinate customer communications.
They accepted an extended, open-ended closure rather than committing to a fixed reopening date, as safety conditions — not a set schedule — determined when it was safe to reopen.
They managed a high volume of cancellations and refunds transparently, keeping clients updated as the situation evolved.
They reopened only once a multi-agency safety assessment confirmed it was safe, over three weeks after the fire began.
They supported the emergency services and local community by providing shelter and meals for those fighting the fires.

title: Focus on play and fun
overview:
Declining mental health and wellbeing is a common side effect of crises. This means that it is all the more important to ensure sport is a place of safety, reprieve and fun. Even sport can become overly serious — more focused on maintaining structure, safety, and logistics than on the enjoyment that draws people to it in the first place. Yet play and fun are one of the most direct ways to support wellbeing when participants are under stress. Playful, low-pressure activity offers a sense of relief, connection, and normality precisely when routines have been disrupted.

Prioritising fun during a crisis also helps sustain participation. When sport starts to feel like an obligation or another source of pressure, dropout can increase. Keeping activities light, flexible, and genuinely enjoyable makes it easier for people to stay engaged, or to return after a break.

guidelines.heading: Adapt the format of activities
items: Reduce emphasis on competition, performance, and results during crisis periods; shift toward participation-focused and game-based formats.
Introduce variety and novelty — new games, informal formats, or mixed-age/mixed-ability sessions — to keep the content of sessions engaging rather than routine.
Allow flexibility in how sessions run (shorter, more frequent, or less structured) to accommodate participants’ changing circumstances and energy levels.

guidelines.heading: Equip coaches to lead with a playful mindset
items: Train coaches and volunteers to recognise when a group needs lighter, more playful sessions. Playful and fun sessions do not need to be without structure.
Encourage coaches to model enjoyment and warmth, not just discipline and performance, especially during stressful periods.

guidelines.heading: Involve participants in shaping activities
items: Ask participants (including children and young people) what kinds of activities they’d enjoy, and build some sessions around their input.
Create space for participant-led games or informal activity, giving people a sense of ownership and control — something often lost during a crisis.

guidelines.heading: Make participation low-barrier
items: Reduce pressure to attend every session or perform at a certain level; welcome participants back without penalty after gaps in attendance.
Offer “come and try” or drop-in style sessions that lower the commitment needed to take part.

guidelines.heading: Check in on wellbeing, not just attendance
items: Use light-touch, informal check-ins (not formal assessments) to gauge how participants are coping, and adjust the tone of sessions accordingly.
Celebrate effort, enjoyment, and participation rather than only results or achievement.

cooperation_guidance: Partner with play and youth-work specialists (e.g. local youth services, play associations) that can offer coaches practical tools and training for running engaging, low-pressure sessions.

Collaborate with other local clubs for joint sessions or activity days to introduce novelty and social connection, while sharing the load of programming during a period when staff and volunteer capacity may be stretched.

Work with schools and community centres who have existing relationships with children and families; partnering with them can help identify participants who may benefit most from playful, welcoming activities and support outreach to those who’ve disengaged.

Engage mental health or psychosocial support organisations to help strike the right balance between fun-focused activity and awareness of participants who may need additional support beyond what sport alone can offer.
